claim: TRACC is a GPCR-based transcriptional recorder of cellular contacts that converts contact events into stable transgene expression.
source: Here, we report TRACC (Transcriptional Readout Activated by Cell-cell Contacts), a GPCR-based transcriptional recorder of cellular contacts, which converts contact events into stable transgene expression.
evidence: This is the primary description of the tool presented in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: TRACC is derived from SPARK and SPARK2.
source: TRACC is derived from our previous protein-protein interaction recorders, SPARK (Kim et al., 2017) and SPARK2 (Kim et al., 2019), reported in this journal.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous publications describing SPARK and SPARK2.

claim: TRACC incorporates light gating via the light-oxygen-voltage-sensing (LOV) domain.
source: TRACC incorporates light gating via the light-oxygen-voltage-sensing (LOV) domain, which provides user-defined temporal control of tool activation and reduces background.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally throughout the manuscript with light-dependent activation data.

claim: The LOV domain provides user-defined temporal control of tool activation and reduces background.
source: TRACC incorporates light gating via the light-oxygen-voltage-sensing (LOV) domain, which provides user-defined temporal control of tool activation and reduces background.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing light-dependent activation and comparison with constructs lacking LOV domain.

claim: TRACC detects cell-cell contacts with high specificity and sensitivity in mammalian cell culture.
source: We show that TRACC detects cell-cell contacts with high specificity and sensitivity in mammalian cell culture and that it can be used to interrogate interactions between neurons and glioma, a form of brain cancer.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2E showing 80.0% specificity and 80.2% sensitivity.

claim: TRACC can be used to interrogate interactions between neurons and glioma.
source: We show that TRACC detects cell-cell contacts with high specificity and sensitivity in mammalian cell culture and that it can be used to interrogate interactions between neurons and glioma, a form of brain cancer.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4 with neuron-glioma co-culture experiments.

claim: Cell-cell interactions are integral to maintaining cellular and organismal homeostasis.
source: Cell-cell interactions are integral to maintaining cellular and organismal homeostasis; signaling that occurs from direct physical cellular contacts mediates a diverse range of biological processes, including embryonic development, neuronal signaling, and immune-cancer interactions (Armingol et al., 2021; Dustin, 2014; Zhang and Liu, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Signaling from direct physical cellular contacts mediates embryonic development, neuronal signaling, and immune-cancer interactions.
source: Cell-cell interactions are integral to maintaining cellular and organismal homeostasis; signaling that occurs from direct physical cellular contacts mediates a diverse range of biological processes, including embryonic development, neuronal signaling, and immune-cancer interactions (Armingol et al., 2021; Dustin, 2014; Zhang and Liu, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LIPSTIC uses sortase A to catalyze labeling on the cell surface of interacting cells.
source: For example, LIPSTIC uses sortase A to catalyze labeling on the cell surface of interacting cells and has been applied to study T cell interactions (Pasqual et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the LIPSTIC publication.

claim: LIPSTIC has been applied to study T cell interactions.
source: For example, LIPSTIC uses sortase A to catalyze labeling on the cell surface of interacting cells and has been applied to study T cell interactions (Pasqual et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the LIPSTIC publication.

claim: The biotin ligase BirA and lipoic acid ligase LplA have been engineered for labeling across synaptic contacts to visualize neuronal synapses.
source: Similarly, the biotin ligase BirA and lipoic acid ligase LplA have been engineered for labeling across synaptic contacts to visualize neuronal synapses (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Split forms of horseradish peroxidase (HRP) have been engineered to perform both extracellular and intracellular labeling at cell-cell contact sites.
source: Split forms of horseradish peroxidase (HRP) (Martell et al., 2016) and the biotin ligase TurboID (Cho et al., 2020; Takano et al., 2020) have also been engineered to perform both extracellular and intracellular labeling at cell-cell contact sites; mGRASP (Kim et al., 2011) and SynView (Tsetsenis et al., 2014) reconstitute GFP across neuronal synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Split forms of the biotin ligase TurboID have been engineered to perform both extracellular and intracellular labeling at cell-cell contact sites.
source: Split forms of horseradish peroxidase (HRP) (Martell et al., 2016) and the biotin ligase TurboID (Cho et al., 2020; Takano et al., 2020) have also been engineered to perform both extracellular and intracellular labeling at cell-cell contact sites; mGRASP (Kim et al., 2011) and SynView (Tsetsenis et al., 2014) reconstitute GFP across neuronal synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: mGRASP reconstitutes GFP across neuronal synapses.
source: Split forms of horseradish peroxidase (HRP) (Martell et al., 2016) and the biotin ligase TurboID (Cho et al., 2020; Takano et al., 2020) have also been engineered to perform both extracellular and intracellular labeling at cell-cell contact sites; mGRASP (Kim et al., 2011) and SynView (Tsetsenis et al., 2014) reconstitute GFP across neuronal synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: SynView reconstitutes GFP across neuronal synapses.
source: Split forms of horseradish peroxidase (HRP) (Martell et al., 2016) and the biotin ligase TurboID (Cho et al., 2020; Takano et al., 2020) have also been engineered to perform both extracellular and intracellular labeling at cell-cell contact sites; mGRASP (Kim et al., 2011) and SynView (Tsetsenis et al., 2014) reconstitute GFP across neuronal synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Direct visualization of cellular contacts is useful, but it is often desirable to also highlight the entire contacting cell for further characterization.
source: While direct visualization of cellular contacts is useful, it is often desirable to also highlight the entire contacting cell, so that cell anatomy, transcriptomic signature, and functional properties can be further characterized.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement that motivates the development of transcriptional reporter tools.

claim: synNotch is a Notch-based system that results in the release of an orthogonal transcription factor in the receiver cell after contact with a sender cell.
source: These include the Notch-based systems synNotch (Morsut et al., 2016) and TRACT (Huang et al., 2017), and the GPCR-based system trans-Tango (Talay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and the context describing TF-based tools.

claim: TRACT is a Notch-based system that results in the release of an orthogonal transcription factor in the receiver cell after contact with a sender cell.
source: These include the Notch-based systems synNotch (Morsut et al., 2016) and TRACT (Huang et al., 2017), and the GPCR-based system trans-Tango (Talay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and the context describing TF-based tools.

claim: trans-Tango is a GPCR-based system that results in the release of an orthogonal transcription factor in the receiver cell after contact with a sender cell.
source: These include the Notch-based systems synNotch (Morsut et al., 2016) and TRACT (Huang et al., 2017), and the GPCR-based system trans-Tango (Talay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and the context describing TF-based tools.

claim: In BAcTrace, the botulinum neurotoxin is transferred to the receiver cell, which results in proteolytic release of a transcription factor.
source: in BAcTrace, the botulinum neurotoxin is transferred to the receiver cell, which also results in proteolytic release of a TF (Cachero et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: In G-baToN, a fluorescent protein is transferred to the receiver cell, which labels the receiver cell.
source: while in G-baToN, a fluorescent protein is transferred, which labels the receiver cell (Tang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: TRACC is comprised of four components.
source: TRACC is comprised of four components, as shown in Figure 1A–B.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A-B.

claim: On the sender cell, a ligand is presented on the cell surface by fusion to pre-mGRASP.
source: On the sender cell, a ligand is presented on the cell surface by fusion to pre-mGRASP, a construct that contains the transmembrane domain of CD4 and the intracellular domain of the pre-synaptic protein neurexin (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: pre-mGRASP contains the transmembrane domain of CD4 and the intracellular domain of the pre-synaptic protein neurexin.
source: On the sender cell, a ligand is presented on the cell surface by fusion to pre-mGRASP, a construct that contains the transmembrane domain of CD4 and the intracellular domain of the pre-synaptic protein neurexin (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: On the receiver cell, a corresponding GPCR is expressed and fused to an LOV domain, a TEV cleavage site, and a transcription factor.
source: On the receiver cell, a corresponding GPCR is expressed and fused to an LOV domain, a TEV cleavage site (TEVcs; ENLYFQM), and a TF.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The receiver cell expresses arrestin fused to the TEV protease.
source: Additionally, the receiver cell expresses arrestin fused to the TEV protease (TEVp) and a reporter construct of interest.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Upon cell-cell contact, the ligand on the sender cell activates the GPCR on the receiver cell, resulting in recruitment of arrestin-TEVp.
source: Upon cell-cell contact, the ligand on the sender cell activates the GPCR on the receiver cell, resulting in recruitment of arrestin-TEVp.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the absence of light, the LOV domain cages the TEVcs, rendering it inaccessible to the TEVp.
source: However, in the absence of light, the LOV domain cages the TEVcs, rendering it inaccessible to the TEVp.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 1A and supported by light-dependent activation data.

claim: With the addition of exogenous blue light, the LOV domain uncages, resulting in subsequent cleavage and release of a transcription factor and reporter activation.
source: With the addition of exogenous blue light, the LOV domain uncages, resulting in subsequent cleavage and release of a TF and reporter activation.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 1A and supported by experimental data.

claim: TRACC is designed as an 'AND' logic gate, simultaneously requiring contact with a sender cell and exogenous blue light.
source: Thus, TRACC is designed as an 'AND' logic gate, simultaneously requiring contact with a sender cell and exogenous blue light.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated by experimental data showing both light and sender dependence.

claim: eLOV is a previously engineered LOV domain that has improved light caging.
source: To first test our design in HEK293T cells, we utilized eLOV, a previously engineered LOV domain that has improved light caging (Wang et al., 2017), and the orthogonal Gal4-UAS TF system.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Six GPCR-ligand pairs were selected that are not expressed or lowly expressed in the brain according to the GTEx database.
source: To ensure that TRACC would be orthogonal for eventual applications in neuroscience, we selected six GPCR-ligand pairs that are not expressed or lowly expressed in the brain according to the GTEx database (Lonsdale et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to the GTEx database.

claim: The six GPCR-ligand pairs tested are CCR3-CCL13, CCR6-CCL20, CCR7-CCL19, GHRHR-GHRH, GNRHR-GnRH, and GCGR-GCG.
source: These are CCR3-CCL13, CCR6-CCL20, CCR7-CCL19, GHRHR-GHRH, GNRHR-GnRH, and GCGR-GCG, the last of which was utilized in trans-Tango (Talay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GCGR-GCG was utilized in trans-Tango.
source: These are CCR3-CCL13, CCR6-CCL20, CCR7-CCL19, GHRHR-GHRH, GNRHR-GnRH, and GCGR-GCG, the last of which was utilized in trans-Tango (Talay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the trans-Tango publication.

claim: The CCR6-CCL20 pair showed the highest ±light and ±ligand signal ratios of 2.6-fold and 3.2-fold, respectively.
source: Of the GPCR-ligand pairs tested, the CCR6-CCL20 pair showed the highest ±light and ±ligand signal ratios (2.6- and 3.2-fold, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A construct omitting the LOV domain showed high background reporter expression and ligand-independent activation with a ±ligand signal ratio of 1.1-fold.
source: Of note, we included a construct that omitted the LOV domain, a design similar to trans-Tango (Talay et al., 2017), and observed high background reporter expression and ligand-independent activation (±ligand signal ratio of 1.1-fold), suggesting that the additional light-gate is crucial for minimizing background.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The additional light-gate is crucial for minimizing background.
source: Of note, we included a construct that omitted the LOV domain, a design similar to trans-Tango (Talay et al., 2017), and observed high background reporter expression and ligand-independent activation (±ligand signal ratio of 1.1-fold), suggesting that the additional light-gate is crucial for minimizing background.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison data showing high background without LOV domain.

claim: In trans assays with HEK293T cells, TRACC showed ±light and ±sender signal ratios of 5.6-fold each.
source: We observed a robust increase in luciferase reporter expression with ±light and ±sender signal ratios of 5.6-fold each.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TRACC was highly specific, with 80.0% of mCherry-expressing cells in direct contact with an HA-positive sender cell.
source: Quantitation of fluorescence intensities of cells across 50 fields of view (FOVs) showed that TRACC was highly specific; of 94 mCherry-expressing cells analyzed, 80.0% were in direct contact with an HA-positive sender cell (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 20% of mCherry-expressing cells were not in direct contact with a sender cell.
source: While we did observe mCherry reporter activation in V5-positive cells not touching sender cells (20% of mCherry-expressing cells were not in direct contact with a sender cell), it is possible that these cells were previously in contact, but the sender cells were dislodged during the course of the experiment or during the washing steps in immunostaining.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Background activation may occur in cells expressing the arrestin-TEVp component at particularly high levels, which can result in GPCR activation-independent release of the transcription factor.
source: It is also possible that background activation may occur in cells expressing the arrestin-TEVp component at particularly high levels, which can result in GPCR activation-independent release of the TF (Sanchez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to published work.

claim: V5 intensity distributions were consistent across high-mCherry and low-mCherry populations.
source: V5 intensity distributions were consistent across high-mCherry and low-mCherry populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that reporter activation is sender-dependent and not a result of differential receiver expression levels.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Reporter activation is sender-dependent and not a result of differential receiver expression levels.
source: V5 intensity distributions were consistent across high-mCherry and low-mCherry populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that reporter activation is sender-dependent and not a result of differential receiver expression levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the V5 intensity distribution data.

claim: 80.2% of receiver cells in contact with sender cells showed reporter expression above background.
source: To assess sensitivity, we determined that 80.2% of receiver cells in contact with sender cells showed reporter expression above background (n = 106 cells from 50 FOVs; above background defined as having a fluorescence signal 1.5-fold or greater above a blank region).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on quantitative analysis of imaging data.

claim: Contacting cells that do not turn on transcription factor may lack one of the other two receiver components (arrestin-TEVp or UAS-mCherry) that need to be co-transfected into the same cell for TRACC to function.
source: One possible explanation for contacting cells that do not turn on TF is that they may lack one of the other two receiver components (arrestin-TEVp or UAS-mCherry) that need to be co-transfected into the same cell for TRACC to function.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental design.

claim: TRACC can be delivered via lentivirus transduction and shows sender- and light-dependent reporter activation.
source: We also performed this experiment using lentivirus transduction instead of transient transfection and similarly observed sender- and light-dependent reporter activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The CCR6 and arrestin receiver components trafficked to neuronal processes as expected.
source: First, we verified that the individual constructs expressed and localized as expected in primary rat cortical neuron culture; we were able to detect the CCR6 and arrestin receiver components and observed that these constructs trafficked to neuronal processes as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The CCL20 sender construct localized properly to pre-synaptic terminals via colocalization with endogenous synapsin.
source: We also verified that the CCL20 sender construct localized properly to pre-synaptic terminals via colocalization with endogenous synapsin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Deletion of the intracellular neurexin domain disrupted the targeting specificity of the sender construct.
source: Deletion of the intracellular neurexin domain disrupted its targeting specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: In neuron culture with cis expression, TRACC showed ±light and ±ligand signal ratios of 11.4- and 7.5-fold, respectively.
source: Approximately 24 hr after 10 min blue light stimulation, we measured luciferase reporter levels on a plate reader and observed robust activation of the TRE-luciferase reporter with high ±light and ±ligand signal ratios of 11.4- and 7.5-fold, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In co-culture with HEK293T receiver cells and neuron sender cells, TRACC showed ±light and ±sender signal ratios of 4.2- and 3.2-fold, respectively.
source: In the luciferase assay, we detected light- and sender-dependent gene expression, with ±light and ±sender signal ratios of 4.2- and 3.2-fold, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: High-grade gliomas are lethal brain cancers and the leading cause of brain tumor death in both children and adults.
source: High-grade gliomas are lethal brain cancers and the leading cause of brain tumor death in both children and adults (Johung and Monje, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Neuronal interactions with glioma cells drive glioma progression.
source: Recent studies have shown that neuronal interactions with glioma cells drive glioma progression (Pan et al., 2021; Venkatesh et al., 2019; Venkatesh et al., 2017; Venkatesh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Gliomas integrate into neural circuits.
source: Gliomas integrate into neural circuits, and one key mechanism driving glioma progression is signaling through functional neuron-to-glioma synapses (Venkataramani et al., 2019; Venkatesh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: One key mechanism driving glioma progression is signaling through functional neuron-to-glioma synapses.
source: Gliomas integrate into neural circuits, and one key mechanism driving glioma progression is signaling through functional neuron-to-glioma synapses (Venkataramani et al., 2019; Venkatesh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In neuron-to-glioma synapses, pre-synaptic neurons communicate electrochemically to post-synaptic glioma cells.
source: In these connections, pre-synaptic neurons communicate electrochemically to post-synaptic glioma cells, and the consequent inward current promotes glioma cell proliferation through membrane voltage-sensitive mechanisms (Venkatesh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The inward current from neuron-to-glioma synapses promotes glioma cell proliferation through membrane voltage-sensitive mechanisms.
source: In these connections, pre-synaptic neurons communicate electrochemically to post-synaptic glioma cells, and the consequent inward current promotes glioma cell proliferation through membrane voltage-sensitive mechanisms (Venkatesh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: SU-DIPG-VI cells stably expressing TRACC components exhibited low sensitivity initially.
source: We observed that SU-DIPG-VI cells stably expressing TRACC components exhibited low sensitivity; only a small fraction of cells showed mCherry reporter expression upon activation of TRACC with recombinant ligand and exogenous blue light (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: eLOV in combination with uTEV2 showed the highest sensitivity in SU-DIPG-VI cells.
source: From screening the SU-DIPG-VI cell lines expressing the different combinations of LOV and TEVp, we found that eLOV in combination with uTEV2 showed the highest sensitivity (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The optimized TRACC activation in DIPG cells was highly specific and required the presence of both recombinant ligand and blue light.
source: Furthermore, while the proportion of cells that became activated increased, this activation was still highly specific and required the presence of both recombinant ligand and blue light (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In co-culture with DIPG receiver cells and neuron sender cells, robust activation of the mCherry reporter was observed only in the presence of both light and sender expression.
source: In this assay, we observed robust activation of the mCherry reporter only in the presence of both light and sender expression in sender neurons (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating the potential to map neuron-glioma cell-cell contact interactions in patient-derived glioma model systems.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TRACC demonstrates the potential to map neuron-glioma cell-cell contact interactions in patient-derived glioma model systems.
source: In this assay, we observed robust activation of the mCherry reporter only in the presence of both light and sender expression in sender neurons (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating the potential to map neuron-glioma cell-cell contact interactions in patient-derived glioma model systems.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the experimental results.

claim: Compared to tools that directly label contact sites, TRACC provides genetic access to contacting cell populations for downstream analysis and potential manipulation.
source: Compared to tools that directly label contact sites such as LIPSTIC (Pasqual et al., 2018), split-HRP (Martell et al., 2016), and mGRASP (Kim et al., 2011), TRACC provides genetic access to contacting cell populations for downstream analysis and potential manipulation.
evidence: This is a comparison statement based on the design of TRACC.

claim: In comparison to synNotch and trans-Tango, the incorporation of light gating in TRACC substantially reduces background signal and provides temporal specificity.
source: Furthermore, in comparison to other TF-based tools like synNotch (Morsut et al., 2016) and trans-Tango (Talay et al., 2017), the incorporation of light gating in TRACC substantially reduces background signal and provides temporal specificity for detecting cell-cell contacts during user-defined time windows.
evidence: This is a comparison statement supported by the experimental data showing light-dependent activation.

claim: The sender construct localizes properly to pre-synaptic terminals.
source: We further showed that TRACC can be applied to detect cellular contacts in both neuron and glioma systems, and that the sender construct localizes properly to pre-synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: TRACC may be useful for synapse-specific tracing, particularly in the anterograde direction (pre-synaptic to post-synaptic).
source: In future studies, TRACC may be useful for synapse-specific tracing, particularly in the anterograde direction (pre-synaptic to post-synaptic) for which tools are currently lacking.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claim: Tools for anterograde synapse-specific tracing are currently lacking.
source: In future studies, TRACC may be useful for synapse-specific tracing, particularly in the anterograde direction (pre-synaptic to post-synaptic) for which tools are currently lacking.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: TRACC will require careful validation of component localization in vivo and testing of specificity and sensitivity in a well-characterized circuit in vivo.
source: This will first require careful validation of TRACC component localization in vivo and testing of TRACC specificity and sensitivity in a well-characterized circuit in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed.

claim: TRACC may be useful for future investigations of neuron-glioma circuitry, allowing identification and subsequent analysis of connected subpopulations.
source: TRACC may also be useful for future investigations of neuron-glioma circuitry, allowing identification and subsequent analysis of connected subpopulations.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.
